content: Froth flotation is a highly selective process used to separate valuable minerals from gangue by employing surfactants and wetting agents. This method enables the economic processing of complex or mixed ores by isolating specific minerals. It is commonly applied to separate sulfides, carbonates, and oxides before further refinement. Additionally, froth flotation is utilized in the processing of phosphates and coal. Beyond mineral processing, this technique is widely employed in industrial wastewater treatment plants to remove fats, oils, grease, and suspended solids. The equipment used for this purpose is known as Dissolved Air Flotation (DAF) units. These units are particularly effective in removing oil from wastewater effluents generated by oil refineries, petrochemical plants, chemical plants, natural gas processing facilities, and similar industrial operations. In 1869, William Haynes patented a process for separating sulfide and gangue minerals using oil, which he termed bulk-oil flotation. Early flotation processes relied on naturally occurring chemicals such as fatty acids and oils, which were used in large quantities as flotation reagents. Over time, the process has evolved to accommodate a broader range of materials, with the introduction of additional collector agents, including surfactants and synthetic compounds, tailored for various applications. The froth flotation process begins with comminution, which involves crushing and grinding the ore to increase its surface area for subsequent processing. This step breaks the rocks into the desired mineral and gangue, which must then be separated. The ore is ground into a fine powder, and the desired mineral is rendered hydrophobic by adding a surfactant or collector chemical. The specific chemical used depends on the mineral being refined; for example, pine oil is used to extract copper. The resulting slurry, or pulp, containing hydrophobic mineral-bearing ore and hydrophilic gangue, is introduced into a water bath that is aerated to create bubbles. The hydrophobic mineral grains attach to the air bubbles, which rise to the surface, forming a froth. This froth is removed, and the concentrated mineral undergoes further refinement. The effectiveness of froth flotation depends on the selective wetting properties of the surfactants used. A suitable surfactant will completely wet one type of particle while only partially wetting another, allowing bubbles to attach to the desired particles and lift them into the froth. The wetting activity of a surfactant can be quantified by measuring the contact angles formed at the liquid/bubble interface. A contact angle of zero indicates complete wetting. For heavier particles, it is crucial to balance the particle's weight with the surfactant adhesion and the buoyant forces of the bubbles to ensure successful flotation. Larger particles can also rise into the froth when buoyed by a swarm of bubbles under appropriate conditions. Froth flotation can be conducted in mechanically agitated cells or tanks, tall flotation columns, and other specialized units such as the Jameson cell. Mechanical cells use a large mixer and diffuser mechanism at the bottom of the tank to introduce air and provide mixing action. Flotation columns, on the other hand, use air spargers to introduce air at the bottom of a tall column while slurry is introduced above. The countercurrent motion of the downward-flowing slurry and upward-flowing air provides mixing. Mechanical cells generally have higher throughput rates but produce lower-quality material, whereas flotation columns have lower throughput rates but yield higher-quality material. The Jameson cell combines slurry with air in a downcomer, where high shear ensures excellent bubble-particle contact without the need for impellers or spargers. In Dissolved Air Flotation (DAF), used in wastewater treatment, air is dissolved into the flotation solution under high pressure. When the solution is released into the flotation chamber, the reduced pressure causes the dissolved air to form bubbles, similar to how dissolved carbon dioxide forms bubbles when a beer bottle is opened. The mechanics of froth flotation involve several key steps: grinding the ore to liberate mineral particles, conditioning the slurry with reagents to achieve hydrophobic surface charges on the desired particles, collecting and transporting the particles upward via bubbles, forming a stable froth on the surface of the flotation cell, and separating the mineral-laden froth from the flotation bath. In a simple flotation circuit, various reagents are added to a mixture of ore and water (pulp) in a conditioning tank. The flow rate and tank size are designed to allow sufficient time for the minerals to be activated. The conditioned pulp is fed into a bank of rougher cells, which remove most of the desired minerals as a concentrate. The rougher pulp then passes to a bank of scavenger cells, where additional reagents may be added. The froth from the scavenger cells is often returned to the rougher cells for further treatment, but in some cases, it may be sent to specialized cleaner cells. The scavenger pulp is typically barren enough to be discarded as tailings. More complex flotation circuits may include multiple sets of cleaner and re-cleaner cells, as well as intermediate re-grinding of pulp or concentrate.
